title: Miles Davis, Eddie Cleanhead Vinson, and WYLD and newscasting
summary: Tex talks about Miles and Dizzy, Eddie Cleanhead Vinson, the blues of relativity, New Orleans radio stations and his network newscasting career.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: What about, uh, what about the, like, Miles Davis?

Yeah, the Miles Davis, yeah. The Miles Davis. The Dizzy Gillespie. The Dizzy Gillespie. The Dizzy Gillespie. I played, I played all of that that way. And then, uh, you know, I was more into a jazz blues kind of thing there for a while, because Eddie Cleanhead Benson had come out with some tunes, because he came out of, uh, trying to think, uh, what band, he came out of the band with, uh, Cootie Williams. He came out of Cootie Williams' band. See? Now, uh, he, he was born in Houston, Texas. And it just so happened that, uh, in 1900, and, uh, I think it was 1971, I was in Houston, Texas, out of club. Ooh, ooh, ooh, that's the way he started that beat, you know, with, uh, you know, with the juice head baby, and all this kind of stuff thrown in your big grass bed. So, uh, so Eddie, I think, was a master craftsman of the alto saxophone, and one of the, uh, I think one of the, the masters of the hard soulful type, uh, blues of relativity. In other words, when I say blues of relativity, that means blues that anybody who had a hard time could relate to. See, this is where blues come in, like, when people think about having a hard time with a woman. But, you know, a lot of people had a hard time, black people had a hard time just living, period. I'm one of the, I'm the first black in the city of New Orleans to broadcast news worldwide from the mutual network. That's it.
